MARKET EVENT PICKER · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER

Which markets and festivals should you work?

The Saturday festival pays the biggest booth fee, but it blocks the morning market and the evening rally that together net more. Paste the events you could do — expected sales, booth fee or percentage cut, travel and hours — and see the exact set that earns the most after costs, with the reason for every event you skip, the break-even sales for each one you keep, and what a fee cut would have to be to change the answer.

For food trucks, market and craft vendors, pop-up shops, caterers, DJs and bands. Nothing is uploaded: the text box is analysed in this browser and never leaves your device.

    Prefer a CLI?

    Same logic, zero dependencies, one command — reads a file or stdin:

    node cli.mjs plan events.csv --cogs 35 --crew-rate 15 --max-per-week 2
cat events.csv | node cli.mjs plan - --json

    Get cli.mjs and engine.mjs — Node 18+, nothing to install, no network call. More: Which markets and festivals are worth your time? The overlap math.

    What's recognised

    InputHandling

    The plan is exact for the numbers you type (search over every allowed combination, up to 24 entangled events at a time). Sales taxes, permits, parking, repeat-customer value and weather are not modelled beyond the one bad-weather check; enter fees and costs as they will really cost you.

    Common questions

    Does it upload my event list?

    No. The browser page works on the text you paste, in your own browser, and never sends it anywhere. The CLI reads a local file or stdin and makes no network call.

    Why skip an event with big sales?

    A big event can overlap two smaller ones that together net more, or use one of your limited weekly slots. The tool compares the total net of every allowed combination and tells you what each swap would cost.

    What counts as an overlap?

    Two events conflict when their times overlap after adding your setup hours before and teardown hours after each, so a market that ends at noon and a festival that opens at 12:30 across town cannot both be worked.

    Is the plan guaranteed to be best?

    It is the exact best answer for the numbers you typed, found by search and checked against trying every combination in the tests. The sales figures are your estimates, so the result is a decision aid, not a forecast. The page also shows what the plan earns if sales come in lower.

    Who is it for?

    Food trucks, craft and farmers-market vendors, pop-up shops, caterers, buskers, DJs and bands, anyone choosing between events that charge a fee or a cut and cannot be in two places at once.

Anonymous feature events (plan_run, example_loaded) are counted only in local storage and can be deleted with the button below. Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control are honoured.

which-markets-and-festivals-to-work.html.text:
Market Event Picker · guide

Which markets and festivals are worth your time? The overlap math

Short answer: pick the set of events that nets the most for the season, not the single event with the biggest sales. An event is worth its sales after cost of goods and any percentage fee, less the flat booth fee, travel and the crew hours it takes including setup and teardown. Two events that overlap cannot both be worked, so the winner is a combination.

A worked example

One Saturday you are offered a big fair and two smaller events. Cost of goods is 35%, crew cost is $15 an hour, setup is 1 hour and teardown half an hour.

  • A Big Fair, 09:00 to 19:00, $4,000 sales, $500 fee, $60 travel. Net $4,000 × 0.65 − $500 − $60 − $15 × 11.5 = $1,867.50.
  • B Morning Market, 08:00 to 12:00, $1,800 sales, $50 fee. Net $1,037.50.
  • C Evening Rally, 14:30 to 21:00, $2,500 sales, $100 fee. Net $1,405.00.

B and C leave room for setup and teardown and are not blocked by each other, but A overlaps both. Together B and C net $2,442.50 against $1,867.50 for A: the biggest event costs $575. The Market Event Picker finds that answer on any list, exactly, and states what each skipped event would cost to swap in.

How the plan is found

  1. Each event gets a net value from your numbers. An event that loses money at your expected sales is never chosen.
  2. Events that overlap once setup and teardown are added, or share a week when you set a weekly limit, form a cluster. Each cluster is searched exhaustively, pruned by what the remaining events could still add.
  3. The tool compares the result with taking events in the order listed and biggest sales first, and re-checks the plan with sales cut to your bad-weather percentage.

Use break-even sales, not hope

Every chosen event shows the sales at which it nets zero. If your honest estimate is close to that number, the event is a bet on weather and foot traffic, and a fee negotiation or a different event may be the better move. The tool also says how much a skipped event's fee would have to drop to take its place.

Questions

Should I take the event with the biggest sales?

Not automatically. Compare the season's total net with and without it: its sales after cost of goods, percentage fee, flat fee, travel and crew hours, minus whatever the events it overlaps or crowds out would have netted.

How do I compare a flat fee with a percentage fee?

Convert both to the sales you actually expect. A $400 flat fee and a 10% cut cost the same at $4,000 in sales; below that the percentage is cheaper, above it the flat fee is. The tool uses your expected sales, and shows each event's break-even sales so you can see how much room you have.

How many events a week is too many?

That is your call, so it is an input: set the most events you will work in a Monday-to-Sunday week and the plan keeps the best ones within it. The tool also warns when a week passes 60 booth and setup hours.

No warranty. This guide is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind. It is not financial, tax, legal or business advice, and you are responsible for verifying its output, for the numbers you enter, and for the terms of any event you apply to. The worked example is illustrative arithmetic, not a forecast of what you will sell.
